extracted.intended_audience: aspiring screenwriters, scriptwriters, and storytellers learning screenplay structure
extracted.subtask_description: Explain and apply Blake Snyder’s Save the Cat 15-beat screenplay structure (three-act model) to craft or analyze feature-length film scripts, including suggested page timings and example beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save the Cat characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Three act structure; Fifteen plot beats; Mostly applied to American Hollywood films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save the Cat is a bestselling screenwriting book by Blake Snyder that condensed successful film structure into a 15-beat three-act model. The article notes the model was compiled from analyzing dozens of successful films and that it’s been used by many writers (and critiqued as potentially formulaic). The characteristics serve as the high-level constraints for applying the beat sheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save the Cat plot device
rubrics_metrics.description: Have the protagonist do something admirable toward the start of the story to establish them as likable and get the audience on their side; the action can be literal or figurative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including a 'save the cat' scene near the start of your script is a quick way to generate empathy and attachment to your main character. Examples may be literal (saving a cat) or symbolic. Anti-patterns/caveats: some critics call this manipulative or cliché, and disagree that protagonists must always be likable or admirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening Image — Page 1
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening image (first scene) establishes the world, the tone, the characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Snyder states the opening image of your film is important because it sets up expectations; nearly every screenplay follows this rule. Use it to convey the story’s baseline visual and emotional state (example: Parasite's opening image conveying a struggling family).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theme Stated — Page 5
rubrics_metrics.description: The main theme of the film should be stated early (around page five).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most good films have a theme, and Snyder advises the main theme should be stated on page five. This can be delivered through a line of dialogue that foreshadows the protagonist’s arc (example: a coworker asking why the protagonist never accepts help). Films can have multiple themes, but the central one should be signposted here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-Up — Pages 1-10
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish the look and feel of the film and introduce the majority of the principal characters while showing the protagonist’s baseline life before it’s disrupted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first ten pages are crucial: set the world rules, tone, and the protagonist’s ordinary world. Use this section to show what the protagonist’s life looks like before the inciting event changes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalyst — Page 12
rubrics_metrics.description: The big inciting incident that turns the protagonist’s life upside down (page ~12).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The catalyst sends the protagonist onto a new trajectory; the character may initially reject it, but by the end of Act One it should propel them to make decisions that start the story in motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debate — Pages 12-25
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist wrestles with whether or not to act after the catalyst; a period of questioning and resistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This section shows the protagonist uncertain about their next steps (examples: denial, rationalization). It spans the remainder of Act One up to the decision that begins Act Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break into Two — Page 25
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist makes the decision that officially launches the main story and moves the narrative into Act Two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This beat is a point-of-no-return choice (literal or figurative) that commits the protagonist to the new world/quest (example: boarding a boat to Antarctica).

rubrics_metrics.name: B Story — Page 30
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce the subplot(s) that will complement or contrast the main story — often the relationship or emotional throughline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The B Story usually begins around page 30 and provides thematic payoff (example: meeting someone who later becomes a partner). It often supports the protagonist’s internal journey and theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fun and Games — Pages 30-55
rubrics_metrics.description: The section where the premise’s promise lives: the protagonist explores the new world or their new abilities; the movie delivers on its concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an amorphous beat where the story shows the rules of the new world and lets the audience enjoy the scenario (examples: Harry Potter exploring Hogwarts). It's where the core 'fun' of your logline should play out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoint — Page 55
rubrics_metrics.description: A major turning point that can be a false victory or a major setback; a big moment that raises the stakes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The midpoint should feel like a significant event — either the protagonist thinks they’ve won (false victory) or they suffer a dramatic loss. Its effect changes the trajectory toward the second half of Act Two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bad Guys Close In — Pages 55-75
rubrics_metrics.description: A period where things get harder for the protagonist; pressures intensify (not always literal antagonists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Following the midpoint, obstacles mount and complications deepen. This beat makes the protagonist's path more difficult, exposing flaws or escalating external opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: All Is Lost — Page 75
rubrics_metrics.description: The nadir for the protagonist: everything appears to be going wrong (the lowest point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the moment of maximum defeat — a loss of mentor, a betrayal, or a shattering failure. It should feel like the character has been punished and may be beyond recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark Night of the Soul — Pages 75-85
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist reacts to the All Is Lost moment and faces despair; they are close to giving up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This beat explores the emotional fallout and reflection; it’s the preparation for the final choice and often includes introspection about the theme and stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break into Three — Page 85
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonist finds a way forward (a renewed sense of purpose or stroke of luck) and commits to the final act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This beat transitions into Act Three: the character decides to try again with new clarity or resources. It often follows a realization or the arrival of a plot device that enables the finale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finale — Pages 85-110
rubrics_metrics.description: The climax where the protagonist applies what they’ve learned and resolves the central conflict; tie up loose ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The finale is the grand culmination of the story—could be a showdown with an antagonist or an internal victory. It should demonstrate the protagonist’s growth and deliver payoff for the earlier beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final Image — Page 110
rubrics_metrics.description: The closing image that leaves the audience with a lasting visual that contrasts or echoes the opening image and reinforces theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This final shot sums up the story and often reflects the protagonist’s changed state (example: The Graduate’s final image). Use it to hammer home the theme and emotional resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usage caveat: Beats are suggestions, not strict rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Snyder’s 15 beats are guidelines; they’re suggestions and not a requirement for a good screenplay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that while many successful writers and scripts follow the beat sheet, adhering to Save the Cat doesn’t guarantee originality or success. Writers should adapt beats to the story they want to tell and be mindful of criticisms that strict adherence can lead to formulaic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other Save the Cat takeaways (loglines and analyses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond the beats and titular device, the book includes logline breakdowns, a formula for writing original loglines, and structural analyses of films.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these additional tools (logline formula, film breakdowns) to refine story concept and marketability. The article references analyses of Interstellar and Parasite as examples of applying the beat sheet.
